title: What We’ve Learned From Our First Looks at the Sixers
contentHtml:
Prepare yourselves: The Eastern Conference will be a roller coaster all season. One day, your team may be on a four-game winning streak and sitting in the no. 3 spot. A week later, it may be clinging to a play-in slot after losing three of four.

It’s a long season, and the new-look Philadelphia 76ers are the ultimate “it’s a long season” team. Every time you are ready to anoint them a superteam in full, favorites in the East, you have to remind yourself of Joel Embiid’s injury history, LeBron James’s age, and that Jaylen Brown arrived in a trade that likely shocked him more than it shocked you.

I remain skeptical that the Sixers can problem-solve their way through three playoff rounds with Embiid looking like he has so far and with injuries and rest nights certainly looming, but they have problem-solved their way to a 2-0 record against the incumbent Eastern Conference finalists—including a rollicking mega-comeback on Thursday night against the always-rickety Cleveland Cavaliers.

Through two games, Embiid is 12-of-31 with five turnovers, and his mobility on defense comes and goes (to put it somewhat generously). He can summon real vertical lift only in dire moments, and sometimes not even then. The backup center position is thin, with Adem Bona getting first crack ahead of Jabari Walker, perhaps Dominick Barlow at points, and then small-ball lineups with James or Dean Wade (who has not played yet) at center.

But the quartet of James, Brown, Tyrese Maxey, and VJ Edgecombe gives Philly a fairly high floor when Embiid struggles or rests, and even presents the possibility of load-managing Embiid through an extended playoff run. (The Ringer’s own Chris Ryan pitched the idea of resting Embiid for Game 1 of the conference semis against the New York Knicks after Philly’s first-round series with Boston went the distance, and my sense is that some among the brain trust in Philly—then and now—did not consider that a wild idea.)

There have been hiccups and bouts of stagnancy in the team’s first two games, but the Sixers are at least trying to push the buttons that will make this superteam hum on offense and survive on defense. Opponents are just 18-of-62 on 3s so far, and that will change, but Philly has hit two absolute musts: limiting turnovers on offense and protecting the glass on defense. Coming into the season, I pegged transition defense and defensive rebounding as potential weak spots, and they may still be, but so far Philly is controlling the parts it can control.

The Sixers have shot even worse on their own 3s—18-of-68—and they created more, and better, open looks from deep than the Knicks in their matchup. Philly isn’t a great long-range shooting team—check Brown’s career numbers on catch-and-shoot 3s for a mild surprise—but they should net out as average-ish from beyond the arc.

Embiid’s 3-point shot is one of the two or three most critical variables that will determine whether Philly is regular good or contender good. He’s 3-of-11 through two games and 199-of-586 (33.9 percent) combined since the start of his 2022-23 MVP season. Can he nudge his way back toward the high 30s? If not, more defenses will start to leave him open instead of stunting at him on pick-and-pops—mini-rotations that leave wings open, provided Embiid makes the right swing pass. But Embiid is the worst 3-point shooter in many of Philly’s core lineups, and when he stands around the arc—as he does a lot now—the Sixers have strong spacing.

In a broader sense, Philly has leaned into the right sort of offensive hierarchy and plopped their star players into the right kinds of places and roles in core set pieces. Those players in turn—especially Brown and Embiid—have so far shown a willingness to spend more time in locations they did not frequent in prior seasons: the corners for both, and the dunker spot for Brown.
